title: the seasons
hook: a clay pot of water by a gate on a hot afternoon: Charaka's summer is about putting back what the sun takes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: spring as the Gita's season of flowers, and Charaka's thaw that asks for lighter food and more movement. Did you choose one lighter thing? Day one thousand three hundred four.

A hot afternoon, somewhere on the plains of north India. Shutters pulled. The street outside nearly empty. By a gate, on a little stand, sits a clay pot, its sides dark and damp, and beside it a steel cup, for anyone walking past. Nobody guards it. Nobody charges for it. The pot sweats, and the water inside stays cool. It's a plain picture of summer, and it holds much of Charaka's summer advice in one object. Today, the hot season.
screen: `A HOT AFTERNOON. SHUTTERS PULLED.` → `A CLAY POT BY THE GATE.` → `TODAY, THE HOT SEASON.`

segments.voice: Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls summer grishma, and its picture, paraphrased, is that the sun's strong rays draw the moisture out of the world, and out of the body along with it. So the answer is to put back what the sun takes. Food and drink that are sweet, cool, liquid, with a little richness. Rice, milk, cooling drinks. And the list of what to go easy on: salty, sour, sharp and hot things, and hard exercise in the heat. Then a small surprise. Elsewhere Charaka is wary of sleeping in the daytime. In summer, he allows it. The nights are short and the days are heavy, so the afternoon rest is part of the cure. Cool rooms, too, and moonlight in the evening. Three things to see here. First, the logic is the one we've followed all along: meet a quality with its opposite. Dry and hot is answered with moist and cool. Second, it's a season for doing less. The advice isn't to push through. It's to slow down and shelter. And third, back to the pot by the gate. Ayurveda's summer says replace what the heat takes from you. The household habit stretches that to whoever walks by. In parts of India, people set out water in the hot months, for strangers, and a shallow dish for birds. Charaka's summer, turned outward. The opposite of the heat, offered to anyone thirsty.
screen: `GRISHMA: THE SUN TAKES` · `PUT THE MOISTURE BACK` · `THE ONE SEASON FOR A NAP` · `A POT OF WATER BY THE GATE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the cool. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring your attention to the tip of the nose. Notice that the in-breath is a little cooler there than the out-breath. Rest on the cool of each inhale. If you're warm, let the forehead soften, the jaw unclench, the hands open on your lap. Nothing to push. If you pray, you can hold in mind someone who is thirsty today, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. In summer, Charaka's reading is a sun that draws out moisture, answered with sweet, cool, liquid food, rest and shade. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Today, give water: drink one full glass slowly, and set one out for someone else, a coworker, a plant, a bird. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda keep summer cool and slow, as the classical texts describe: sweet, cool, liquid food and drink, less hard exercise, and rest in the heat; in parts of India households set out water for passersby and birds in the hot months.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6 (grishma: the sun draws out moisture; sweet, cold, liquid, unctuous food and drink; avoid salty, sour, pungent, hot things and exercise; day sleep, cool places, moonlight)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 21 (day sleep generally discouraged, permitted in summer)

notes: Charaka Sutrasthana 6 grishma regimen: confirm the paraphrase (sun's rays draw out moisture; sweet, cold, liquid, unctuous food; rice and milk; avoid salty, sour, pungent, hot and exercise; cool rooms; moonlight). The text also mentions wine, diluted or avoided; omitted here. The 'nights are short' reason for summer day sleep is from Sutrasthana 21; confirm.
Day sleep: confirm that Charaka (Sutrasthana 21, and the summer regimen in Sutrasthana 6) permits day sleep in grishma while discouraging it otherwise.

'In parts of India, people set out water in the hot months, for strangers, and a shallow dish for birds' (pyau / water stalls): confirm wording. The clay pot scene in the hook is an illustrative scene, not a claim about any one place.
